title: The Fast Sheet

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Sixteenth Saying: A shortcut is a road that someone else will have to pay for.*

The dust on the road from the Salt Flat did not settle; it hovered, a fine grey silt that coated the tongue and the gears of the instruments. Isla wiped her sightglass with the hem of her coat, a gesture that Mags, watching from the cookfire, deemed a waste of good wool. They had been out of the Pale for two days, the land behind them still shifting in its slow, lazy drift, when the caravan appeared.

It was not a caravan of necessity. It was a caravan of confidence. A dozen men in matching slate-grey coats marched in perfect step, their boots striking the packed earth with a rhythmic, military precision that made Joss’s teeth ache. Their wagon was lacquered black, fitted with brass fittings that gleamed in the morning sun, and on its side, painted in gold leaf, was the Royal crest: a lion rampant holding a compass.

At the head of the procession rode a man on a white horse, his coat pristine, his face smooth and unlined. He held a whip in one hand, though he did not use it, and in the other he held a leather portfolio bound in red. He reined his horse to a stop ten paces from Isla’s tripod, and the dust from his hooves settled on her field-book.

"Good morning," he said. His voice was soft, the sort of softness that suggests the speaker has never once been told 'no' and is therefore surprised by the concept. "I am Lyle Corwin. I am the Deputy Surveyor to the Lord Chancellor. You must be Master Vasht’s apprentice."

Isla looked at the red portfolio, then at the dozen men behind him, who were already unpacking cases of instruments that looked more like jewelry than tools. She straightened her back, ignoring the ache in her shoulders from the last three days of triangulation.

"I am Isla Corrin," she said. "And I am the surveyor. Master Vasht is at base camp, resting his ankle."

Corwin smiled. It was a practiced smile, symmetrical and empty. "How kind of you to step in. The Chancellor is aware of the delay. He is also aware of the deadline. Midsummer is not a suggestion, Miss Corrin; it is a statute. But perhaps, with our combined resources, we might finish sooner than anyone expects." He nodded toward his wagon. "We have a plan."
pages.image: A dusty road where a man in a pristine slate-grey coat sits on a white horse, holding a red portfolio, smiling at a girl in a mustard-yellow canvas coat who stands beside a brass tripod, her face stern and ink-stained.

pages.text:
They called it the Fast Sheet. Corwin unrolled it on the top of a flat stone, smoothing the edges with hands that did not seem to believe they might tear the paper. The sheet was beautiful. That was the first thing that struck Isla. The lines were clean, the contours were elegant, the legends were precise. It looked like a work of art, a picture of a country that had been tidied up, like a room where every object had been placed to hide the mess.

Isla leaned over the sheet, her nose almost touching the ink. She traced the line of the river, the Wend, with her finger. It curved in a smooth, logical arc. She looked at the contour lines, the thin brown rings that marked the height of the land. They were evenly spaced, perfectly concentric, suggesting a gentle, uniform slope.

"It is elegant," she said, and the word tasted like ash.

"Efficiency is elegance," Corwin said, folding one corner of the sheet. "We have used standard gradients. The land here is, ostensibly, flat. We have estimated the distances by pacing, calibrated for the terrain. The angles were read once, with high-precision sextants. There is no need for redundancy when the initial data is sound."

Isla’s mind moved faster than her mouth. Pacing. Once. She looked at the sheet again. She found the location of the Pale, the drifting fog-plain, and then she looked for the valley. Ennis Vale. It was there, tucked into a fold of the land. But the contour lines around it were not what she had seen. They were not the gentle, rolling shape of a valley floor. They were tight, deep, plunging inward. The lines suggested a basin. A deep, enclosed basin.

She pulled out her own field-book, the pages soft with use, the numbers written in her small, cramped hand. She compared her notes on the elevation of the mill-race with the contours on Corwin’s sheet. The discrepancy was not a hair’s breadth. It was a foot. Then two. Then ten.

"The river," she said, her voice quiet. "You have put the river at the bottom of this basin. If you seal this sheet, the river will flow into the valley. It will fill it."

Corwin looked at her, his expression one of mild amusement, as if she had pointed out a spelling error in a letter. "It is a reservoir," he said. "A natural one. The Chancellor has plans for water management in the Marches. It is a feature of the plan, Miss Corrin, not a flaw in it."

Isla looked at the valley on the sheet. It was no longer a home. It was a bucket.
pages.image: A close-up of a hand tracing a line on a map where contour lines form a deep, tight basin, with a smaller, rougher field-book open beside it showing conflicting numbers, the paper pristine and the other worn.

pages.text:
Corwin did not speak of money. He spoke of progress, a word that seemed to smooth the rough edges of the world until they were ready for filing. He stood with his hands clasped behind his back, watching the Pale where the fog rolled in, soft and grey, erasing the boundary of the known.

"The Chancellor sees the Unmade not as a wilderness," he said, "but as a resource. There is grain waiting to be grown. There is water waiting to be held. The Marches are overpopulated. The land is tired. We are giving it purpose. We are giving it shape."

"And the people?" Isla asked. "The ones who are already there. The ones who have lived there for forty-four years."

Corwin turned to her. His eyes were clear, and that clarity was the frightening part. There was no malice in them, only a pragmatic, efficient indifference. "The Chancellor has provided for them. There is a fund. Generous compensation. They will be moved to cottages in Vell, near the Guild, where they can be part of the city. It is a kindness, Miss Corrin. They will no longer have to live in the drift. They will have stability."

"They do not want to leave," Isla said. "They have a mill. They have a school. They have a bell. They have a life."

"They have a location," Corwin corrected. "And a location is a line on a map. If the line is drawn differently, the location changes. That is the nature of the work. We do not ask the land for permission. We tell it what it is. And it obeys."

Isla felt a coldness settle in her stomach, a heavy, sinking weight that threatened to pull her under. She thought of Perrin’s hands, rough and scarred, gripping the bell rope. She recalled the children in the schoolroom, their voices echoing off the slate walls. She remembered the orchard, the apples red against the green, the way the light caught the leaves in the morning.

"You are not telling the land what it is," she said. "You are telling it what you want it to be. And the ink will believe you. Because you will not check."

Corwin’s smile did not waver. "The ink believes the truth, Miss Corrin. And the truth is that this sheet is finished. It is complete. It is ready."
pages.image: A man in a grey coat standing with his back to a girl in a mustard coat, looking out at a rolling grey fog, his posture rigid and formal, the girl’s profile sharp with anger in the foreground.

pages.text:
Isla walked back to the camp as the river’s rushing sound filled her ears, a drowning rhythm that would not stop. She did not sleep that night. Instead, she sat by the cookfire, watching the flames dance while her mind remained blank. The air above the fire shimmered and warped, a visual distortion she could measure but not explain. The tent ropes pulled taut against the wind, holding the fabric steady through sheer tension.

Her thoughts turned to the baseline. She recalled the chain, which had to be held taut not by brute force, but by precision. If it sagged, the measurement was wrong. If she ignored the sag, the number became a lie. In the Unmade, a lie was not an abstract concept. It was a physical slope. It was a river forced to run uphill. It was a valley twisted into a reservoir.

She picked up her pen and opened the field-book, but she did not write. She merely held the instrument, feeling the small, brass weight of the nib against her fingertips. Corwin had said the Queen would receive the sheet that was finished. He had not said the sheet that was true. In the Guild, truth was not a virtue one simply possessed. It was a method. It was the rigorous process of checking, verifying, and refusing to let a number stand until it had been proven redundant.

Isla watched the fire again. The flames were chaotic and alive, yet if she closed her eyes and let that chaos go, the fire would either die or burn out of control. There was no middle ground. There was no compromise between a steady flame and a blaze.

She stood up. Her legs were stiff from the cold, but her mind was clear. She had a job to do. Not to finish the work, but to check it. To prove the figures. To show the work.

She walked to her tent and pulled out the theodolite. The metal was cold to the touch, biting into her palm as she carried it out. She set it up on the tripod, adjusted the bubble level until it centered in the glass, and looked through the sight. The world beyond the firelight was sharp, clear, and defined by the crosshairs.

She began to read the angles.
pages.image: A girl in a mustard coat standing by a tent at night, setting up a brass instrument on a tripod, the firelight casting long shadows, her face illuminated and focused, the dark forest behind her.

pages.text:
Sera found her an hour later, appearing at the edge of the firelight without a sound, her plum-purple velvet coat dark in the twilight and the slim silver rule in her breast pocket catching the last of the moon’s glow. She looked tired, but not from physical labor; it was the specific exhaustion of a mind that had been running too fast on a track that was too narrow.

"I saw the sheet," Sera said, her voice low and stripped of its usual sharpness. "I saw it in the Chancellor’s office, before he sent it to you. I thought it was beautiful. I thought it was efficient. I thought it was good."

She sat down on a log, her polished black boots scraping against the dirt, and did not look at Isla. Instead, she watched the way the sparks rose from the coals and died in the cold air.

"I was taught that a map must be quick," Sera continued. "That speed is the measure of skill. That if you can do it in a day, you are a master. If you take a week, you are a failure. I have spent three years believing that. I have built my whole life on that belief."

She turned to Isla, her eyes dry but bright with a fierce, defensive intensity. "But I looked at the contours. And I knew they were wrong. I knew them in my hands, in the way the pen felt when I drew the line. It was forced. It was a lie. And I did not check. I did not check because checking takes time. And time is wasted."

Isla looked at her, seeing the same fear she had felt on the roof, in the Atlas Room, and under the drifting fog of the Pale. It was the fear of being merely adequate, of being slow, of letting a number stand until it had been proven redundant.

"I do not know any other way to be good," Sera whispered. "I do not know how to be good if I am not fast. I do not know how to be good if I am not right. And I am not right. I am not fast. I am only... me."

Isla reached out and placed her hand on Sera’s arm. It was a small gesture, but it was solid. It was a line, drawn and held.

"Then let me teach you the slow way," Isla said. "And you can tell me if it was worth it."

Sera looked down at Isla’s hand, then up at her face. For the first time, the sharpness in her eyes softened. It did not disappear, but it changed. It became something else. Something that could hold.
